assignment.title: Anesthesia — analgesia, sedation and pharmacology

taxonomy.title: Anesthesia — analgesia, sedation and pharmacology
taxonomy.scopeIn: Airway/sedation safety, anesthetic and analgesic mechanisms, interactions and toxicity, neuromuscular blockade/reversal, MH and laparoscopic anesthetic physiology.
taxonomy.scopeOut: General ICU ventilation belongs to critical-respiratory-ventilation. Chronic perioperative medication reconciliation belongs to perioperative-risk-recovery. Transplant drug mechanism belongs to transplant-immunosuppression.
taxonomy.priorityReason: A bounded perioperative lane covers important mechanisms with direct management consequences.
researchAgenda: MH and drug interactions with exact evidence support
taxonomy.coverageReason: Live identities cover part of this scope. The research agenda flags breadth to check, and the topic worker must judge redundancy and question quality.
taxonomy.testingWeightBasis: Owner-directed editorial estimate of general-surgery testing relevance. No exam percentages or official blueprint weights are asserted.

concepts.displayName: Recognize systemic local-anesthetic toxicity
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize a compatible neurologic or cardiac toxicity pattern after supplied local-anesthetic exposure in a completed outside-care event.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Distinguish paralysis from anesthesia
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize that neuromuscular blockade produces skeletal-muscle relaxation without itself providing unconsciousness or analgesia.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Explain local-anesthetic nerve blockade
concepts.learningObjective: Identify voltage-gated sodium-channel blockade as the principal mechanism interrupting sensory nerve excitation and conduction.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Boosted ART and midazolam
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize increased midazolam exposure with ritonavir or cobicistat and coordinate route-specific sedation planning.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Apply benzodiazepine-antagonist contraindication after seizure control
concepts.learningObjective: Use the actual indication for perioperative midazolam to choose a reversal plan when supported respiratory depression competes with preservation of treatment for a potentially life-threatening seizure state.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Insufflation CO2 absorption
concepts.learningObjective: Explain a documented gradual CO2 rise during uncomplicated pneumoperitoneum by systemic absorption of insufflated gas rather than assuming an unrelated acute catastrophe.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Pneumoperitoneum and respiratory compliance
concepts.learningObjective: Relate increased airway pressure during evaluated pneumoperitoneum to cephalad diaphragm displacement and reduced respiratory compliance.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Quantitative blockade recovery assessment
concepts.learningObjective: Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring rather than head lift, apparent strength or visual twitch count alone to assess recovery from blockade.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Sugammadex pharmacologic selectivity
concepts.learningObjective: Identify rocuronium and vecuronium as the blockers selectively complexed by sugammadex rather than assuming universal relaxant reversal.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Explain absorbed laparoscopic CO2
concepts.learningObjective: Explain the extra blood CO2 load and potential respiratory acidemia from peritoneal absorption of insufflated CO2 when reviewing a completed outside laparoscopic operation.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Integrate venous and acid-base observations
concepts.learningObjective: Use a reversible position change and a persistent arterial-gas pattern to distinguish two simultaneous laparoscopy physiology mechanisms.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Separate gas direction from demonstrated acidemia
concepts.learningObjective: Interpret a controlled positional filling response and distinguish an acidifying gas change from an acidemic state using laboratory intervals.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Interpret a paired pressure challenge
concepts.learningObjective: Integrate controlled circulatory observations with ventilator-pressure observations to distinguish venous-return and respiratory-mechanics explanations.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Plan trigger-free anaesthesia for MH susceptibility
concepts.learningObjective: Arrange specialist trigger-free anaesthetic and facility planning for known or credibly documented MH susceptibility.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Integrate familial MH risk with all components of a proposed anaesthetic
concepts.learningObjective: Interpret a documented first-degree susceptibility result despite prior uneventful exposure, then distinguish triggering drugs across anaesthetic components.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Choose the surgical testing sequence under unresolved familial MH risk
concepts.learningObjective: Interpret family history and an uninformative genetic result, then distinguish nontriggering perioperative planning from prophylactic dantrolene or obligatory preoperative contracture testing.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Respiratory recurrence after naloxone
concepts.learningObjective: Choose continued monitored respiratory care after an opioid-reversal response rather than infer durable recovery from the first improvement.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Ventilation despite a reassuring saturation display
concepts.learningObjective: Select assessment of ventilation when sedation-associated respiratory depression is obscured by a reassuring oxygen-saturation display.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Motor reversal versus full anesthetic recovery
concepts.learningObjective: Keep hypnotic and opioid recovery assessment separate after documented reversal of rocuronium blockade.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Two missing quantities in recovery
concepts.learningObjective: Select complementary assessments of ventilation and current oxygen-carrying quantity when a saturation display and an earlier hemoglobin result are insufficient.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: A normal twitch ratio after a second blocker
concepts.learningObjective: The first twitch recovered after the original reversal, then fell after a different blocker without marked fade. Do not apply rocuronium reversal to that new depolarizing-agent pattern.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Acquiring intermittent ventilation events
concepts.learningObjective: A nasal signal gap coupled to mouth position is not yet evidence that ventilation stopped; saturation on oxygen cannot decide it. Acquire the missing expiratory route at the same event time instead of substitute a between-event or slow trend value.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Repeated respiratory recurrence during opioid reversal
concepts.learningObjective: Reproducible short respiratory responses coexist with painful over-reversal after a larger peak. Choose titratable ongoing antagonism rather than repeatedly increase or reproduce bolus peaks.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Explain naloxone's receptor action
concepts.learningObjective: Explain competitive opioid receptor antagonism in patient-specific naloxone counseling or review of completed emergency care.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Interpret pneumoperitoneum venous return
concepts.learningObjective: Explain pressure-associated venous compression while accounting for position and phase instead of assuming pneumoperitoneum always changes preload in one direction.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Explain reassuring referred shoulder pain
concepts.learningObjective: Explain a diaphragmatic/phrenic contributor to mild improving shoulder pain after laparoscopy only when current assessment is reassuring and warning features remain explicit.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

concepts.displayName: Arrange adult support after endoscopic sedation
concepts.learningObjective: Plan responsible adult collection and support after sedated gastroscopy rather than self-driving or unaccompanied travel and recovery.
concepts.assignmentBasis: Organ/decision-family assignment reviewed against the topic scope.

decisionNodes.stem: Which mechanism best explains the documented CO2 rise during this patient's pneumoperitoneum?

answerChoices.label: Peritoneal absorption of insufflated CO2
Pulmonary uptake of newly inspired CO2
Metabolic production from rising body temperature

decisionNodes.stem: Which acid-base effect matches the supplied CO2 and pH changes during this patient's completed operation?

answerChoices.label: Respiratory acidemia from a greater CO2 load
Metabolic acidemia from greater lactate production
Respiratory alkalemia from greater CO2 loss
Metabolic alkalemia from greater bicarbonate gain

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Respiratory acidemia from a greater CO2 load.” Absorption during pneumoperitoneum can add to the respiratory CO2 burden; the supplied record does not establish a lactate-driven event or prescribe a ventilator setting.

decisionNodes.stem: Which paired interpretation best fits {patientName}'s record?

answerChoices.label: Reduced cardiac filling; increased respiratory elastic load
answerChoices.rationale: Smaller filling volume with preserved ejection fraction supports reduced preload rather than a new loss of contractility. The increased plateau pressure at the same delivered volume supports an elastic-load component.

answerChoices.label: Reduced cardiac contractility; increased respiratory elastic load
answerChoices.rationale: The respiratory interpretation fits. Smaller end-diastolic volume with similar ejection fraction does not best support primary loss of contractility as the explanation of lower stroke volume.

answerChoices.label: Reduced cardiac filling; increased respiratory resistive load
answerChoices.rationale: The filling interpretation fits. A new resistive load does not by itself account for the higher plateau pressure under the supplied ventilation controls.

answerChoices.label: Reduced cardiac contractility; increased respiratory resistive load
answerChoices.rationale: Both are real contributors to perioperative deterioration, but neither is the best primary account of the supplied paired observations.

decisionNodes.explanation: The fall in stroke volume accompanies a smaller end-diastolic volume with a similar ejection fraction, supporting reduced filling rather than new primary contractile failure. Higher plateau pressure at unchanged tidal volume and PEEP indicates an increased elastic pressure requirement. The reversible pressure sequence fits abdominal venous-return restriction and respiratory mechanical restriction, without proving a unique vascular lesion or excluding every mixed mechanism.

decisionNodes.stem: Which paired conclusion should be carried into {patientName}'s anaesthetic review?

answerChoices.label: Position-associated reduction in filling; acidemia not demonstrated
answerChoices.rationale: The filling change reverses with position at fixed pressure. The CO2/pH directions are compatible with an acidifying change, but the later pH is within the laboratory interval, not acidemic.

answerChoices.label: Position-associated reduction in filling; respiratory acidemia demonstrated
answerChoices.rationale: The filling interpretation fits, but a lower pH that remains within the laboratory interval does not establish acidemia.

answerChoices.label: Pressure-associated reduction in filling; acidemia not demonstrated
answerChoices.rationale: The gas conclusion fits. Assigning the reversible change to a pressure increase is not supported when pressure stays fixed and position is reversed.

answerChoices.label: Pressure-associated reduction in filling; respiratory acidemia demonstrated
answerChoices.rationale: This pair overstates both the pressure attribution and the absolute gas conclusion. Neither follows from the supplied sequence.

decisionNodes.explanation: The smaller filling and stroke volumes reverse on returning flat at unchanged pressure, supporting a positional contribution. CO2 rises and pH falls, but both later measurements lie within their laboratory intervals. That direction of change does not establish acidemia. The earlier low-CO2/high-pH state matters: describing a change as acidifying is different from diagnosing a later acidemic state. These controlled observations do not prescribe a ventilator or fluid adjustment.

decisionNodes.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes monitored IV from oral midazolam with boosted ART?

answerChoices.label: IV use needs reviewed dosing and monitoring
IV use can proceed under the unchanged dose plan
Oral substitution is preferable to monitored IV use
IV use calls for withholding the ART regimen

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “IV use needs reviewed dosing and monitoring.” Parenteral midazolam may be considered with appropriate monitoring and individualized dose review; oral restrictions should not be copied wholesale. Changing route does not erase the need to assess increased exposure. The oral route has the contraindication; monitored parenteral use is assessed differently. ART interruption is not the default solution to an interaction requiring sedation planning.

decisionNodes.stem: What explains the warning about prolonged midazolam effects with boosted protease-inhibitor therapy?

answerChoices.label: Reduced CYP3A clearance of midazolam
Reduced intestinal absorption of midazolam
Increased renal elimination of midazolam
Increased hepatic metabolism of midazolam

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Reduced CYP3A clearance of midazolam.” Booster-mediated metabolic inhibition can increase and prolong exposure. Reduced absorption would not explain prolonged increased midazolam exposure. Greater elimination does not explain the metabolic interaction. The interaction reduces rather than increases CYP3A-mediated metabolism.

decisionNodes.stem: What is the best response to an unexplained ART omission when oral therapy is feasible?

answerChoices.label: Reconcile and continue the prescribed ART
Continue the postoperative ART hold
Restart the first listed ART component
Restart the ward single-drug ART substitute

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Reconcile and continue the prescribed ART.” An omission calls for coordinated medication reconciliation, not a routine postoperative hold. The unexplained hold should be reconciled when administration is feasible. A partial regimen is not coordinated ART continuation. Uncoordinated partial substitution does not restore the prescribed regimen.

decisionNodes.stem: Which mechanism explains the midazolam interaction with cobicistat?

answerChoices.label: Inhibition of CYP3A-mediated metabolism
Increased renal elimination of midazolam
Reduced intestinal absorption of midazolam
Induction of CYP3A-mediated metabolism

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Inhibition of CYP3A-mediated metabolism.” Reduced metabolism can increase midazolam exposure and prolong sedation. The booster warning concerns metabolic inhibition rather than increased renal elimination. Reduced absorption does not explain increased exposure from CYP3A inhibition. The relevant booster effect inhibits rather than induces midazolam metabolism.

decisionNodes.stem: Which source of CO2 load supports the anesthesiologist's explanation of this completed uncomplicated course?

answerChoices.label: Absorption of the insufflation gas
Circuit rebreathing of exhaled CO2
Increased metabolic CO2 from hyperthermia
Reduced alveolar ventilation from tube obstruction

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Absorption of the insufflation gas.” The insufflated CO2 can enter the systemic circulation. The completed course includes a functioning assessed circuit rather than rebreathing. The course is described as evaluated and uncomplicated rather than a hyperthermic metabolic event. The documented course excludes a new airway obstruction.

decisionNodes.stem: Which effect explains the pressure-volume change rather than the added CO2 load itself?

answerChoices.label: Reduced compliance from cephalad diaphragm movement
Increased compliance from a caudally displaced diaphragm
Improved compliance from greater diaphragm excursion
Expansion of lung volume without altered respiratory mechanics

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Reduced compliance from cephalad diaphragm movement.” Gas absorption and restrictive mechanics are distinct consequences of insufflation. The documented pressure requirement points toward restriction. The documented mechanical effect reduces rather than improves expansion and compliance. The pressure-volume relation changed in this course.

decisionNodes.stem: Which effect of abdominal insufflation is consistent with the documented reduction in respiratory compliance?

answerChoices.label: Upward diaphragm displacement restricting lungs
Downward diaphragm displacement freeing lung expansion
Expansion of resting lung volume without pressure effects
Removal of chest-wall restriction by increased abdominal pressure

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Upward diaphragm displacement restricting lungs.” Mechanical compression changes respiratory expansion. This would not match the restrictive physiology. The summary specifically describes reduced compliance. Increasing abdominal pressure can impose restriction instead.

decisionNodes.stem: Which mechanical effect explains a greater pressure requirement for the same tidal volume during evaluated pneumoperitoneum?

answerChoices.label: Cephalad diaphragm shift with lower compliance
Caudal diaphragm shift with greater compliance
Increased lung volume with unchanged chest mechanics
Increased chest compliance with easier lung expansion

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Cephalad diaphragm shift with lower compliance.” Abdominal insufflation can restrict respiratory expansion. That is the opposite of the described restrictive effect. The pressure-volume change reflects altered mechanics. Greater compliance would not explain the increased pressure requirement.

The completed course includes a functioning assessed circuit rather than rebreathing. The course is described as evaluated and uncomplicated rather than a hyperthermic metabolic event. The documented course excludes a new airway obstruction. The correct answer is “Cephalad abdominal displacement limiting expansion.” Position and insufflation can accentuate diaphragm-related restriction. That does not match head-down insufflation physiology. The situation restricts rather than frees expansion. The abdomen is insufflated rather than decompressed.

decisionNodes.stem: Which monitoring plan specifically improves assessment of recovery from neuromuscular blockade?

answerChoices.label: Plan quantitative neuromuscular monitoring
Assess sustained voluntary head lift
Assess repeated voluntary hand-grip strength
Assess train-of-four twitches by visual inspection

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Plan quantitative neuromuscular monitoring.” Objective monitoring directly addresses residual blockade assessment; other emergence checks still remain necessary. Clinical strength does not replace objective recovery measurement. Clinical strength can miss residual blockade. Visible twitch assessment is qualitative rather than quantitative.

decisionNodes.stem: Which correction best addresses the claim that sugammadex binds every neuromuscular blocker?

answerChoices.label: Its binding is selective for rocuronium and vecuronium
Its binding applies equally to cisatracurium and succinylcholine
Its binding applies equally to atracurium and mivacurium
Its binding applies equally to rocuronium and succinylcholine

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Its binding is selective for rocuronium and vecuronium.” The selectivity should not be extrapolated to cisatracurium. The stated universal selectivity is incorrect. Specific binding should not be generalized to other blocker classes. Including a different blocker makes this claimed selectivity incorrect.

decisionNodes.stem: Why can hypnotic sedation persist after sugammadex reverses rocuronium blockade?

answerChoices.label: Blocker binding leaves propofol sedation
Sugammadex accelerates propofol elimination
Sugammadex directly binds circulating propofol
Sugammadex antagonizes propofol at its receptor

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Blocker binding leaves propofol sedation.” Neuromuscular reversal and emergence from hypnosis are different processes. Blocker complex formation does not establish accelerated hypnotic clearance. The represented binding targets are neuromuscular blockers, not propofol. Blocker binding is not direct reversal of hypnotic receptor effects.

decisionNodes.stem: Which information is more useful than a visible twitch count for judging blockade recovery?

answerChoices.label: Quantitative train-of-four ratio
Sustained bedside head-lift assessment
Voluntary bedside hand-grip assessment
Qualitative assessment of twitch fade

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Quantitative train-of-four ratio.” Four visible responses alone do not quantify residual fade adequately. A clinical strength test does not quantify residual blockade. Clinical strength can appear adequate despite residual blockade. Subjective fade assessment is less accurate than quantitative measurement.

decisionNodes.stem: Which mechanism explains sugammadex reversal of vecuronium-induced blockade?

answerChoices.label: Complex formation with circulating blocker
Increased acetylcholine release at the motor nerve
Competitive displacement at nicotinic receptors
Inhibition of acetylcholine breakdown at the junction

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Complex formation with circulating blocker.” Binding reduces free vecuronium available at the neuromuscular junction. Sugammadex acts through blocker binding rather than increasing transmitter release. The represented mechanism is complex formation with blocker rather than receptor competition. Sugammadex binding is distinct from an anticholinesterase mechanism.

decisionNodes.stem: Which drug in this completed anesthetic record is specifically complexed by sugammadex?

answerChoices.label: Rocuronium
Cisatracurium
Succinylcholine
Atracurium

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Rocuronium.” Sugammadex selectively binds this steroidal neuromuscular blocker. Sugammadex binding selectivity for rocuronium and vecuronium should not be extrapolated to this blocker. This is not one of the blockers selectively complexed by sugammadex. The labeled rocuronium and vecuronium selectivity does not establish reversal of this blocker.

decisionNodes.stem: Which general-anaesthetic regimen should be proposed for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Propofol infusion with remifentanil; rocuronium for intubation
answerChoices.rationale: The first-degree family result warrants managing the patient as potentially susceptible until assessed. An uncomplicated previous exposure does not establish absence of susceptibility. This regimen avoids both volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine.

answerChoices.label: Sevoflurane maintenance with fentanyl; cisatracurium for intubation
answerChoices.rationale: This is a familiar anaesthetic regimen and reproduces a drug previously tolerated, but sevoflurane remains an MH trigger. A prior uneventful anaesthetic does not clear the family-history risk.

answerChoices.label: Propofol infusion with fentanyl; succinylcholine for intubation
answerChoices.rationale: Intravenous maintenance can be suitable, but the induction/intubation component also matters: succinylcholine remains a trigger. A plan is not made trigger-free merely by replacing the maintenance agent.

decisionNodes.explanation: The first-degree family result warrants managing the patient as potentially susceptible until assessed. An uncomplicated previous exposure does not establish absence of susceptibility. This regimen avoids both volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine. This is a familiar anaesthetic regimen and reproduces a drug previously tolerated, but sevoflurane remains an MH trigger. A prior uneventful anaesthetic does not clear the family-history risk. Intravenous maintenance can be suitable, but the induction/intubation component also matters: succinylcholine remains a trigger. A plan is not made trigger-free merely by replacing the maintenance agent.

decisionNodes.stem: Which recommendation should be sent to {patientName}'s anesthesia team?

answerChoices.label: Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia; arrange contracture testing separately
answerChoices.rationale: The uneventful exposure and negative panel do not clear susceptibility in this family. With the represented nontriggering plan and documented MH preparation, definitive susceptibility testing need not become a prerequisite to surgery.

answerChoices.label: Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia; administer prophylactic dantrolene
answerChoices.rationale: This retains an appropriate intravenous technique but adds prophylaxis as though familial risk requires pretreatment even with trigger avoidance and MH preparation. It confuses readiness to treat a crisis with routinely administering the rescue drug.

answerChoices.label: Plan propofol–remifentanil anesthesia after muscle-contracture testing
answerChoices.rationale: The family result and negative panel justify continued risk precautions, not necessarily delaying surgery until a definitive susceptibility test is completed. This is a credible sequencing error when an inconclusive genetic result is treated as a barrier to a nontriggering anesthetic.

decisionNodes.stem: Which sequence of venous effects best explains the two phases in {patientName}'s record?

answerChoices.label: Abdominal venous emptying, then restriction of caval inflow
answerChoices.rationale: Initial displacement of blood centrally can augment filling, whereas greater pressure can impede venous return; the reversal with pressure reduction supports that context-dependent sequence.

answerChoices.label: Restriction of caval inflow, then abdominal venous emptying
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the direction of venous effects needed to explain the observed rise and subsequent fall in filling.

answerChoices.label: Dependent venous pooling, then increased central venous return
answerChoices.rationale: This predicts the opposite filling sequence and would require a different positional/venous context.

decisionNodes.explanation: Initial compression of abdominal venous reservoirs can move blood centrally, while greater abdominal pressure can impede caval return. The observed ventricular-volume and stroke-volume changes fit that sequence here. Pneumoperitoneum does not have one universal circulatory effect; pressure, circulating volume and position matter.

decisionNodes.stem: Which paired physiological explanation best accounts for {patientName}'s recorded response?

answerChoices.label: Caval return restriction with reduced respiratory compliance
answerChoices.rationale: The reversible pressure association supports impaired abdominal venous return. A matched rise in peak and plateau pressures at the same tidal volume fits mechanical compliance restriction rather than a new resistive component.

answerChoices.label: Positional venous pooling with reduced respiratory compliance
answerChoices.rationale: The respiratory component fits, but the table position did not change; this pair assigns the circulation change to the wrong recorded variable.

answerChoices.label: Caval return restriction with increased airway resistance

decisionNodes.stem: Which paired interpretation best fits {patientName}'s later observations?

answerChoices.label: Positional venous pooling and CO2-related respiratory acidemia
answerChoices.rationale: The reversible position-linked volume changes support head-up reduction in venous return; the persistent CO2/pH/bicarbonate pattern supports a separate respiratory CO2-load effect.

answerChoices.label: Pressure-related caval compression and CO2-related respiratory acidemia
answerChoices.rationale: The gas interpretation fits, but assigning the reversible later volume change to a pressure increase contradicts the recorded constant pressure and position reversal.

answerChoices.label: Positional venous pooling and fixed-acid metabolic acidemia
answerChoices.rationale: The volume interpretation fits; the blood-gas pattern does not support new fixed acid as the primary explanation when CO2 rises and bicarbonate is unchanged.

answerChoices.label: Pressure-related caval compression and fixed-acid metabolic acidemia
answerChoices.rationale: Both are real physiological categories, but neither best matches the independently recorded position response and gas pattern.

decisionNodes.explanation: Head-up positioning can reduce venous return despite the earlier central-volume rise after insufflation. Recovery on flattening at constant abdominal pressure supports a positional contribution. The independent higher-CO2/lower-pH pattern with unchanged bicarbonate fits respiratory acidemia rather than a new primary fixed-acid process. Absorbed insufflation CO2 can contribute to that load, which need not reverse with the table position.

decisionNodes.stem: Which nerve most likely carries the initiating afferent signal for {patientName}'s postoperative pain pattern?

answerChoices.label: Phrenic nerve
answerChoices.rationale: The postoperative shoulder-tip pattern with preserved local function supports referred pain from diaphragmatic irritation through phrenic afferents.

answerChoices.label: Vagus nerve
answerChoices.rationale: A visceral pathway is a credible competing thought after abdominal surgery, but it does not explain this characteristic diaphragm-associated shoulder referral as well.

answerChoices.label: Suprascapular nerve
answerChoices.rationale: This is a local shoulder competitor, but the timing and preserved movement/power favor a referred source over a local shoulder-nerve injury.

answerChoices.label: Supraclavicular nerves
answerChoices.rationale: This is a credible alternative at the perceived pain site, but the question asks for the initiating afferent rather than the local sensory distribution.

decisionNodes.explanation: Diaphragmatic irritation after laparoscopy can produce shoulder-tip pain through phrenic sensory afferents. decisionNodes.stem: Which ART plan is appropriate when the prescribed regimen can be continued perioperatively?

answerChoices.label: Continue ART with the perioperative team
Withhold ART during surgical recovery
Use a single-drug ART formulary substitute
Continue the unboosted ART components

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Continue ART with the perioperative team.” Routine surgery alone is not an indication to stop effective ART. Surgical recovery alone does not justify interrupting feasible ART. An uncoordinated single-drug substitute does not preserve the prescribed regimen. Uncoordinated removal of part of a regimen is not the continuity plan.
sourceLabels: Perioperative Care in Adults With HIV

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The medication review now identifies ritonavir-boosted ART and a proposed oral midazolam order at the outside surgical service.
decisionNodes.stem: What is the appropriate response to proposed oral midazolam with ritonavir-boosted ART?

answerChoices.label: Revise sedation for the ART interaction
Retain the planned oral midazolam order
Increase the proposed oral midazolam dose
Withhold the ART regimen for oral sedation

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Revise sedation for the ART interaction.” Boosted therapy can increase midazolam exposure; this oral combination requires an alternative plan. The oral combination has a route-specific contraindication. Increased exposure from metabolic inhibition does not support a dose increase. A coordinated alternative sedation plan is preferable to sacrificing feasible effective ART.

decisionNodes.stem: Which combined mechanical effect explains increased respiratory restriction in this evaluated course?

answerChoices.label: Cephalad abdominal displacement limiting expansion
Caudal abdominal displacement enlarging resting lung volume
Greater compliance from unrestricted diaphragm descent
Increased resting lung volume from an empty abdomen

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Cephalad abdominal displacement limiting expansion.” Position and insufflation can accentuate diaphragm-related restriction. That does not match head-down insufflation physiology. The situation restricts rather than frees expansion. The abdomen is insufflated rather than decompressed.

decisionNodes.stem: Which naloxone strategy best addresses {patientName}'s repeated course while preserving a titratable respiratory endpoint?

answerChoices.label: Naloxone maintenance infusion
answerChoices.rationale: Repeated transient responses support ongoing antagonism; titration can address recurrent respiratory depression without repeatedly seeking complete analgesic reversal.

answerChoices.label: Larger intermittent naloxone boluses
answerChoices.rationale: The larger bolus caused substantial pain yet did not sustain respiratory recovery; simply increasing bolus peaks does not address the recurring gaps.

answerChoices.label: Unchanged intermittent naloxone boluses
answerChoices.rationale: The prior regimen repeatedly left recurrent respiratory depression between doses; it is a stabilization measure rather than the best ongoing strategy in this record.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret both the reproducible response and its duration. Each naloxone administration restores spontaneous breathing, but the effect repeatedly ends before the respiratory problem resolves. A larger peak also removes useful analgesia. During continued respiratory support, a titrated infusion is the best offered ongoing antagonist strategy. This does not prescribe a dose, infusion formula, interval or discharge criterion; anesthesia review must confirm the exact application.

decisionNodes.stem: Which added recording best determines whether the brief gaps in {patientName}'s trace represent pauses in ventilation?

answerChoices.label: Combined oral-nasal expired-gas waveform
answerChoices.rationale: Capturing oral as well as nasal expired gas at the event time distinguishes a sampling-route gap from a true ventilation pause.

answerChoices.label: Between-event arterial carbon-dioxide sampling
answerChoices.rationale: A between-event arterial value can assess gas exchange then but cannot establish whether each brief missing waveform was a respiratory pause.

answerChoices.label: Transcutaneous carbon-dioxide concentration trending
answerChoices.rationale: A slower concentration trend does not resolve the route and timing of a brief missing expired-gas waveform.

decisionNodes.explanation: A saturation fraction during oxygen delivery does not resolve ventilation. Nor does a missing nasal expired-gas trace necessarily establish apnea when the sampling route changes. Acquire oral and nasal expired gas with synchronized observation before interpreting the short gaps as respiratory pauses. A blood gas or transcutaneous trend may answer a different sustained gas-exchange question. The acquisition priority and placeholder wait classification require anesthesia/source review; the clinic does not execute these hospital recordings.

decisionNodes.stem: Which extubation and reversal plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded reassessment?

answerChoices.label: Continued assisted ventilation with sugammadex dosing complete
answerChoices.rationale: The quantitative motor response has returned to its baseline, but the respiratory observations do not establish recovery from the other drugs. Continued ventilatory support is required.

answerChoices.label: Tracheal extubation to oxygen with sugammadex dosing complete
answerChoices.rationale: The blocker endpoint does not establish adequate spontaneous ventilation or recovery from hypnotic/opioid effects.

answerChoices.label: Continued assisted ventilation with further sugammadex administration
answerChoices.rationale: Support is appropriate, but the measured motor response does not establish a further rocuronium-reversal requirement.

answerChoices.label: Tracheal extubation to oxygen with further sugammadex administration
answerChoices.rationale: Neither an additional blocker-specific agent nor supplemental oxygen establishes recovery of spontaneous ventilation.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the quantitative motor result separately from spontaneous respiratory performance. The measured twitch ratio is back at the pre-block value, while spontaneous breathing is shallow and CO2 is elevated. Sugammadex does not reverse the other anesthetic drug classes. Maintain assisted ventilation and reassess those effects rather than use motor reversal or oxygen administration as extubation clearance.

decisionNodes.stem: Which blocker-directed plan best fits {patientName}'s final recording during continued ventilation?

answerChoices.label: Await recovery from the depolarizing agent
answerChoices.rationale: The near-equal depressed twitches after the second agent do not demonstrate recovery merely because their ratio resembles baseline; sugammadex does not reverse succinylcholine.

answerChoices.label: Give additional sugammadex for residual rocuronium
answerChoices.rationale: This anchors on the original drug and ratio while ignoring the second agent and the intervening return of twitch amplitude.

answerChoices.rationale: This interprets the current weakness as residual nondepolarizing fade rather than the newly recorded depolarizing pattern.

proposedCases.name: Lena Ortiz
proposedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 46-year-old woman, reviews an outside operative record in clinic after recovery. During bupivacaine wound infiltration she developed metallic taste, ringing ears, confusion and then hypotension. Injection stopped; the outside team secured ventilation and began lipid emulsion and circulatory support. Generalized convulsions now continue while blood pressure remains low despite support.

nodes.objective: Choose seizure control during continuing cardiovascular compromise.
nodes.task: Which drug should Lena Ortiz's outside team select for the ongoing convulsions while ventilation and circulatory support continue?

choices.label: Titrated intravenous midazolam
choices.rationale: A benzodiazepine is preferred for seizures in local-anesthetic toxicity. Titrate with airway and circulatory support; it can also depress breathing.
choices.temptation: Select a seizure treatment that fits the toxic exposure and compromised circulation.
choices.counterfactual: This supported toxicity-associated seizure is the represented indication.

choices.label: Titrated intravenous propofol
choices.rationale: Propofol can suppress seizures, but it can aggravate cardiovascular depression. Persistent hypotension favors a benzodiazepine when available. Small incremental propofol remains a fallback in some guidance, not an absolute contraindication.
choices.temptation: Use a familiar rapidly acting anticonvulsant anesthetic despite the current circulation.
choices.counterfactual: If a benzodiazepine were unavailable, small incremental propofol could be considered with appropriate support and attention to circulation.

choices.label: Titrated intravenous thiopental
choices.rationale: Historical guidance includes small incremental thiopental, but current AHA/ASRA guidance prefers benzodiazepines for this toxicity. The present circulatory compromise does not justify choosing a less-supported anesthetic alternative first.
choices.temptation: Choose another anticonvulsant anesthetic familiar from refractory seizure care.
choices.counterfactual: Lack of the preferred benzodiazepine could make a carefully titrated alternative relevant under specialist guidance.

nodes.objective: Choose a cardiac toxicity adjunct without adding another local anesthetic.
nodes.task: Which additional toxicology-directed medication is reasonable for Lena Ortiz's recurrent rhythm while electrical treatment, lipid therapy and resuscitation continue?

choices.label: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
choices.rationale: AHA describes bicarbonate as a reasonable adjunct for life-threatening wide-complex tachycardia from local-anesthetic toxicity. This addresses the exposure/conduction problem during, not instead of, electrical and supportive treatment.
choices.temptation: Match the current conduction abnormality to the toxic exposure.
choices.counterfactual: The represented life-threatening local-anesthetic-associated broad-complex rhythm is the conditional indication.

choices.label: Intravenous lidocaine
choices.rationale: Lidocaine is familiar from other ventricular-arrhythmia care, but adding another local anesthetic is avoided during local-anesthetic systemic toxicity.
choices.temptation: Apply a generic ventricular-arrhythmia drug without adapting to the poisoning.
choices.counterfactual: A ventricular arrhythmia in an appropriate non-local-anesthetic setting could make lidocaine reasonable under resuscitation guidance.

choices.label: Intravenous magnesium sulfate
choices.rationale: The described uniform rhythm does not show the polymorphic twisting pattern associated with torsades; magnesium does not address the demonstrated local-anesthetic sodium-channel toxicity as directly.
choices.temptation: Treat every broad-complex rhythm as a magnesium-responsive torsades event.
choices.counterfactual: A recurrent polymorphic rhythm with a prolonged QT interval would support magnesium while electrical treatment continues.

nodes.explanation: Interpret the current electrical observations in the context of bupivacaine toxicity. The broad uniform complexes and recurrent poor perfusion support a toxicity-directed bicarbonate adjunct rather than another local anesthetic or a torsades-directed choice. proposedCases.name: Priya Shah
proposedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old woman, reviews an outside anesthetic in clinic. Cisatracurium was used. With surgery complete, a checked quantitative adductor-pollicis monitor records two responses to train-of-four stimulation; a four-response ratio cannot yet be obtained. The tracheal tube, anesthesia and assisted ventilation remain in place. There is no immediate requirement to reverse paralysis.

nodes.objective: Use blocker identity and measured depth to select when to antagonize cisatracurium.
nodes.task: Which blocker-reversal plan best fits Priya Shah's recorded checkpoint while anesthesia, ventilation and quantitative monitoring continue?

choices.label: Await further spontaneous recovery before neostigmine/glycopyrrolate
choices.rationale: Two twitches indicate more block than the minimal recovery state preferred for reliable neostigmine antagonism. Maintain support and reassess spontaneous recovery before selecting its administration point.
choices.temptation: Integrate the actual blocker and current depth rather than select a drug from its name alone.
choices.counterfactual: At minimal block, neostigmine/glycopyrrolate with quantitative reassessment becomes an appropriate antagonist plan.

choices.label: Give neostigmine/glycopyrrolate at the present block depth
choices.rationale: Neostigmine can antagonize cisatracurium after sufficient recovery, but success is unlikely at fewer than four twitches. With no urgent reversal requirement, giving it at this depth is less reliable than allowing more recovery first.
choices.temptation: Recognize the correct antagonist but ignore the depth-dependent timing.
choices.counterfactual: Four twitches with sufficiently recovered quantitative transmission would make administering neostigmine/glycopyrrolate reasonable.

choices.label: Give sugammadex at the present block depth
choices.rationale: Sugammadex does not target cisatracurium. Its ability to reverse deeper aminosteroid blockade does not transfer to this blocker.
choices.temptation: Transfer a reliable deeper-block reversal strategy across blocker classes.
choices.counterfactual: With rocuronium or vecuronium rather than cisatracurium, sugammadex could be an appropriate depth-dependent strategy.

nodes.explanation: The blocker identifies which antagonist can work, but the two-response depth determines when to rely on neostigmine. Continue anesthesia and support, allow more spontaneous recovery and use quantitative measurements to select and verify antagonism. The guidance describes unreliable reversal at fewer than four twitches, not an absolute neostigmine prohibition or a fixed waiting interval.

authorGate.interpret: Recognize that two measured train-of-four responses are not the minimal block at which neostigmine is most reliable.
authorGate.apply: Use the cisatracurium identity to reject sugammadex and choose supported waiting/reassessment before neostigmine when urgent reversal is unnecessary.
authorGate.closestError: Give the chemically appropriate neostigmine immediately without considering the measured block depth.

proposedCases.name: Hannah Cole
proposedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 48-year-old woman, reviews an outside laparoscopic anesthetic in clinic. At the recorded checkpoint, the surgeon has just increased insufflation pressure. Position, fluids, anesthetic dosing, delivered tidal volume, inspiratory flow and measured total PEEP are unchanged. Ventilator pressure readings use passive inspiratory holds. An intraoperative transesophageal echocardiogram obtained by the anesthetist records ventricular volumes and ejection fraction. Arterial pressure has fallen and peripheral perfusion has worsened. No pressure-reduction trial has yet been performed.

nodes.objective: Integrate current ventricular-filling and passive respiratory-pressure findings after a controlled insufflation-pressure increase.
nodes.task: Which change should Hannah Cole's surgeon and anesthetist make next at this checkpoint while perfusion and ventilation are supported?

choices.label: Lower insufflation pressure and reassess
choices.rationale: Reduced filling and stroke volume with similar ejection fraction, together with increased passive plateau pressure at fixed ventilation, support a trial reducing the new pressure burden. Reassess rather than assume a guaranteed response or sole cause.
choices.temptation: Integrate circulatory filling and respiratory elastic-load findings with the controlled pressure change.
choices.counterfactual: The represented new pressure burden with these observations supports the trial.

choices.label: Give an inhaled bronchodilator and reassess
choices.rationale: Both peak and passive plateau pressures rise at fixed volume, flow and total PEEP; this is not the isolated resistive-pressure increase that would make bronchospasm the best initial explanation. The lower filling is also unexplained by that choice.
choices.temptation: Treat a high peak airway pressure as bronchospasm without using the plateau measurement.
choices.counterfactual: A rise confined chiefly to the peak-minus-plateau gradient with compatible wheeze/flow findings would support bronchodilator treatment.

choices.label: Begin myocardial inotropic support and reassess
choices.rationale: Smaller ventricular filling with similar ejection fraction does not chiefly demonstrate a new contractility failure. Addressing the just-increased pressure burden is more directly supported before attributing the decline to pump weakness.
choices.temptation: Read a smaller stroke volume as isolated myocardial contractile failure.
choices.counterfactual: Newly impaired ventricular systolic function despite adequate filling would strengthen an inotropic-support indication.

nodes.explanation: The observations are pre-intervention. Smaller filling and stroke volume with similar ejection fraction favor a filling-related contribution; the passive plateau rise indicates added elastic load rather than isolated airway resistance. With the other stated conditions unchanged, trial a lower insufflation pressure and reassess both systems. No successful pressure-reduction response is supplied in advance, and persistent deterioration would require further evaluation.

authorGate.interpret: Infer reduced filling rather than primary systolic failure from the volume/ejection observations, and elastic load rather than isolated resistance from the passive plateau rise.
authorGate.apply: Use the common new pressure exposure to select a reversible pressure-reduction trial with reassessment rather than an isolated bronchodilator or inotrope response.
authorGate.closestError: Give a bronchodilator for the raised peak pressure or an inotrope for the reduced stroke volume without integrating plateau and filling measurements.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The filling/stroke-volume decline and plateau rise occur immediately after a controlled pressure increase, with position, ventilation, PEEP and dosing unchanged.
authorGate.counterfactual: A peak rise with a stable plateau and compatible airflow findings would support bronchodilator treatment; depressed systolic function despite adequate filling would strengthen the inotrope alternative.
authorGate.cueAttack: Removed every after-reduction/return-toward-prior finding. All options propose an unperformed next intervention and reassessment. The acquisition and passive measurement conditions are explicit.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without plateau the resistance competitor gains plausibility; without filling/ejection data the inotrope competitor is not resolved. No option can be selected by repeating an already successful intervention.

proposedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 59-year-old man, reviews an outside gastroscopy event in clinic. Topical benzocaine was used. During recovery his lips looked dusky and pulse oximetry stayed low despite oxygen, although its waveform matched his pulse. An arterial gas showed high oxygen tension with near-normal calculated saturation. Ventilation and circulation were being assessed and supported.

nodes.objective: Interpret discordant oxygen measurements after oxidant exposure and select confirmation.
nodes.task: Which additional measurement should Samuel Grant's outside team have requested?

choices.label: Arterial co-oximetry with measured hemoglobin fractions

choices.temptation: Resolve the discrepancy with the relevant direct measurement.
choices.counterfactual: The oxidant exposure and discordance apply.

choices.label: Repeat arterial gas with calculated oxygen saturation
choices.rationale: A repeated saturation calculated from dissolved oxygen does not directly measure the suspected fraction.
choices.temptation: Treat calculated saturation as an independent hemoglobin measurement.
choices.counterfactual: Changing ventilation or dissolved oxygen could justify repeating a gas, while the fraction question still requires measurement.

choices.label: Second-site two-wavelength pulse oximetry

choices.temptation: Assume relocating a reliable sensor changes its measurement principle.
choices.counterfactual: A poor peripheral signal could justify another site for signal reliability.

proposedCases.name: Samuel Grant
proposedCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 59-year-old man, reviews an outside hospital event in clinic. Following benzocaine-associated methemoglobinemia, the hospital administered methylene blue. At a later reassessment he has dyspnea at rest, tachycardia and marked pallor. Hemoglobin has fallen from 11.4 to 5.6 g/dL, indirect bilirubin has risen and haptoglobin is low; the direct antiglobulin test is negative. Current co-oximetry places methemoglobin within the laboratory reference interval. G6PD activity is below reference. No active bleeding is found. Further methylene blue is withheld, and respiratory/circulatory support continues.

nodes.objective: Distinguish post-treatment symptomatic hemolytic anemia from persistent methemoglobinemia and select the current oxygen-delivery treatment.
nodes.task: Which additional treatment best addresses Samuel Grant's current oxygen-delivery problem at this reassessment?

choices.label: Transfuse packed red blood cells
choices.rationale: The current severe symptomatic hemoglobin loss with the nonimmune hemolytic pattern, after the measured methemoglobin fraction has normalized, supports red-cell replacement. The drug label notes that methylene-blue-associated anemia may require transfusion.
choices.temptation: Treat the demonstrated current loss of functional hemoglobin rather than the prior abnormal fraction.
choices.counterfactual: The represented symptomatic severe anemia is the relevant target; no universal transfusion cutoff is being authored.

choices.label: Administer intravenous ascorbic acid
choices.rationale: Ascorbic acid is a possible alternative for life-threatening methemoglobinemia when methylene blue is contraindicated or unavailable. It does not directly replace the large current hemoglobin deficit, and the measured fraction is now within reference.
choices.temptation: Continue treating the previous dyshemoglobin disorder because the usual antidote is now unsuitable.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent life-threatening methemoglobinemia with a methylene-blue contraindication could make ascorbic acid relevant under toxicology guidance.

choices.label: Arrange red-cell exchange transfusion
choices.rationale: Exchange transfusion may be considered for life-threatening methemoglobinemia unresponsive to methylene blue. That persistent abnormal-fraction problem is not shown here; direct red-cell replacement more closely addresses the current anemia without requiring exchange.
choices.temptation: Choose an escalation for refractory methemoglobinemia after seeing an antidote complication.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent life-threatening methemoglobinemia despite treatment could support an exchange-transfusion consultation.

nodes.explanation: The present problem is severe symptomatic hemolytic anemia: the hemoglobin quantity has fallen markedly, the hemolysis pattern is nonimmune, and current measured methemoglobin is within reference. Transfuse red cells while support and evaluation continue. The low G6PD result supports the methylene-blue safety concern, but it does not choose among these alternatives; the current anemia versus dyshemoglobin findings do. Do not give another antidote merely for the historical diagnosis.

authorGate.interpret: Interpret the falling hemoglobin, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin and negative antiglobulin pattern as a current hemolytic-anemia problem and reconcile it with a now-normal methemoglobin fraction.
authorGate.apply: Choose red-cell replacement for the current symptomatic hemoglobin deficit rather than alternative treatment for ongoing refractory methemoglobinemia.
authorGate.closestError: Choose ascorbic acid or exchange treatment for the old methemoglobinemia solely because methylene blue is now unsafe.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Severe symptomatic hemoglobin loss is current, while co-oximetry shows the methemoglobin fraction within reference; methylene blue is already withheld in every plan.
authorGate.counterfactual: If hemoglobin quantity were preserved but life-threatening methemoglobinemia persisted with methylene blue contraindicated, an alternative fraction-directed treatment would become relevant.
authorGate.cueAttack: All choices are concrete oxygen-delivery treatments. Withholding methylene blue is shared background, and the G6PD result no longer eliminates two repeat-dose distractors. No residual-elevation treatment threshold is assumed.
authorGate.deletionTest: Deleting G6PD does not select a treatment; deleting the current hemoglobin/fraction comparison destroys the distinction between replacement and dyshemoglobin-directed rescue.

His outside record describes failed direct laryngoscopy, subsequent difficult video-assisted intubation, and mask ventilation requiring two clinicians plus an oral airway. Neck radiotherapy has left restricted mouth opening and limited extension. He breathes comfortably at rest and cooperates with examination. The anesthesia team is comparing airway-securing strategies.

nodes.objective: Integrate anticipated intubation and rescue-ventilation difficulty when choosing airway sequence.
nodes.task: Which airway strategy should Isaac Miller's anesthesia team plan?

choices.label: Secure the trachea awake before inducing general anesthesia
choices.rationale: Prior intubation and ventilation difficulty together favor maintaining spontaneous breathing during airway security.
choices.temptation: Use the rescue history as well as laryngoscopy history.
choices.counterfactual: The cooperative patient with these anticipated risks applies.

choices.label: Induce general anesthesia before attempting video-assisted intubation
choices.rationale: A video device does not remove the represented post-induction ventilation risk.
choices.temptation: Treat eventual prior video success as evidence induction is low risk.
choices.counterfactual: Reliable ventilation and a favorable current assessment could support an induced strategy after risk comparison.

choices.label: Induce general anesthesia before placing a supraglottic airway
choices.rationale: Changing devices after induction does not itself resolve the anticipated combined risk.
choices.temptation: Assume an alternative device guarantees rescue ventilation.
choices.counterfactual: A suitable procedure with an assessment supporting reliable supraglottic ventilation would change the plan.

nodes.explanation: Read intubation difficulty and ventilation rescue together. Prior difficulty with both persists in a cooperative patient with continuing anatomical limitations. The awake-securing strategy is the best offered sequence; the anesthesia team chooses the device, topicalization, sedation and rescue details.

authorGate.apply: Secure the airway before induction instead of relying on another device afterward.

authorGate.counterfactual: A current assessment establishing reliable ventilation and easier airway access could support an induced video-assisted strategy.

originalReview.title: MH family risk and surgical testing sequence
fairness: Proceeding with the represented nontriggering pathway while arranging specialist assessment is the best offered recommendation. A prior uneventful exposure and a negative panel without a known familial variant do not resolve the affected sibling's risk.

Two consequential decisions remain: interpret the family/testing evidence, then distinguish safe anesthetic preparation from a requirement to finish diagnostic testing. Testing-first and prophylactic dantrolene are recognizable competing errors.

The readiness details are necessary conditions for the proposed action, not an instruction that it is safe to proceed. They should not be deleted merely to make the question harder. First node; no preceding explanation supplies its answer.
